Previous work has demonstrated a significant correlation between the pattern of sea level change 20

computed from an altimeter-based inference of Greenland ice mass flux from 1993-2019 and sea 21

surface height (SSH) observations adjacent to the island. However, a key question is unanswered 22

in this detection; namely, what constraints on ice mass flux do the SSH observations provide? To 23

address this issue, we perform a series of inversions of the available SSH data offshore 24

Greenland. Our results indicate that such inversions are highly non-unique. However, we also 25

demonstrate that robust inferences can be obtained by incorporating reasonable a-priori 26

constraints, in our case limiting the ice model to a small set of discs associated with the major 27

drainage basins of the ice sheet that are proximal to the SSH observations. Our inversions in this 28

case yield estimates of average ice mass loss in the range 0.62-0.70 mm/yr in units of equivalent 29

global mean sea level change over the period 1993-2019, when the observations are corrected for 30

the signal of dynamic sea level change. This inference agrees with independent ice altimeter- 31

based estimates of Greenland ice sheet mass flux rates, showing broadly consistent relative ice 32

mass loss rates across southern Greenland basins. Our analysis is the first to directly invert SSH 33

observations for ice mass changes and we conclude that the consideration of such data, 34

particularly in combination with other data sets (e.g., GRACE gravity, ice altimeter 35

measurements, GNSS observations) has the potential to improve constraints on ice sheet mass 36

changes in a warming world. 37

1. Introduction 38

The first modern treatment of post-glacial sea level changes dates back a half century (Farrell 39

and Clark, 1976) and a study highlighting the unique geometry of sea level changes in response 40

rapid ice mass flux, as expected in a warming world, followed only one year later (Clark and 41

Lingle, 1977). Renewed attention in the latter topic (e.g., Conrad and Hager, 1997; Mitrovica et 42

al., 2001, 2011; Plag and Jüttner, 2001; Bamber and Riva, 2010; Spada and Galassi, 2016; 43

Moreira et al., 2021; Coulson et al., 2022) was motivated, at least in part, by the explosion of 44

observational constraints on sea level change that supplemented the coastal tide gauge record 45

(Holgate et al., 2013), including the launch of the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite altimetry mission 46

(Fu et al., 1994) and numerous follow-on missions (see Hamlington et al., 2023). Interest in the 47

geometry of rapid sea level changes also arose from their counterintuitive nature. Sea level will 48

fall within ~2000 km from a rapidly melting ice sheet due to uplift of the unloaded crust and the 49

loss of gravitational attraction between the ice sheet and ocean, and it will generally rise at 50

progressively greater distances, although rotational effects on sea level are overprinted on the 51

latter geometry. The near field fall in sea level can reach an amplitude several orders of 52

magnitude greater than the global mean sea level (GMSL) rise associated with the melt event, 53

while the far-field the sea level rise can exceed GMSL by up to 30-35%. Since each pattern of 54

ice mass change in ice sheets or glaciers yields a unique geometry of sea level change, the latter 55

have come to be known as sea level fingerprints (Plag and Jüttner, 2001), and the power of these 56

fingerprints is that they introduce the possibility of using sea level observations to move beyond 57

estimates of GMSL change to constrain the source(s) of meltwater (e.g., Mitrovica et al., 2001). 58

59

Detecting sea level fingerprints in the modern ocean is challenging given the large, confounding 60

signals associated with sterodynamic processes and the similarity of the spatial structure of 61

fingerprints from different melt sources (e.g., Greenland vs Iceland; Hay et al., 2017). A 62

modeling analysis (Kopp et al., 2010) argued that detecting the sea level fingerprint of the 63

Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) melting at a rate comparable to the last few decades (~0.5 mm/yr of 64

GMSL rise) would require ~30 years of altimeter observations of sea surface height (SSH) 65

change below 66°N. Studies have reported detections of the GrIS fingerprint based on tide gauge 66

records along the US East coast (Davis and Vinogradova, 2017), a decade of altimeter records in 67

the North Atlantic corrected for steric effects (Moreira et al., 2021) and ocean bottom pressure 68

data from sensors in the tropics (Hsu and Velicogna, 2017). However, these far-field datasets are 69

characterized by low signal-to-noise ratios. In contrast, Coulson et al. (2022) investigated the 70

GrIS fingerprint using a newly expanded altimeter database that extends to 78°N and includes 71

the ocean surrounding all but the northern edge of Greenland. After applying a correction for the 72

sterodynamic (ocean-circulation-driven) signal, they found a significant correlation (p < 0.001) 73

between a fingerprint computed using an altimeter-based estimate of GrIS mass flux from 1993- 74

2019 (Simonsen et al., 2021) plus a model reconstruction of glacier mass changes at the 75

periphery of Greenland (Malles and Marzeion, 2021) and the observed SSH change around 76

Greenland. 77

78

The correlation results reported by Coulson et al. (2022) provide an unambiguous detection of 79

the GrIS fingerprint but do not address a key question, namely, what is the inherent information 80

content of the SSH observations regarding the GrIS mass change from 1993-2019? That is, what 81

robust constraints do these observations provide on the modern ice sheet evolution? To answer 82

this question, we describe here the results of the first formal geophysical inversion of altimeter- 83

based SSH data for ice mass changes. The mapping between SSH data and ice mass changes is 84

non-unique, in large part because of the limited resolving power of the data. However, we 85

demonstrate that with some reasonable a-priori constraints on ice geometry, the inversion 86

provides robust constraints on ice mass changes that are consistent with independent data sets 87

(e.g., GRACE gravity data and direct altimeter-based estimates of ice mass changes, as in 88

Simonsen et al., 2021). 89

3. Results & Discussion 157

Examples of Fréchet kernels for a set of sites that sample the western, southern and eastern ocean 158

~ 100 km from Greenland, are shown in Figure 1B-F. The gradients in kernels are greatest close 159

to the site, reflecting the deformational and gravitational anomalies underlying the response to 160

the adjoint loads. As expected, the amplitude of each kernel quickly decays as one move further 161

away from the observation site, and becomes negative at greater distances. Across the GrIS the 162

kernels are smooth and have a low amplitude and shallow gradient, thus one would expect, even 163

with a large number of SSH observations, that spatial resolution across the GrIS will be 164

relatively poor. 165

The non-uniqueness implied by this limited resolving power has important implications for the 173

inverse problem. In the initial application of the inversion procedure, we discretized the area 174

covered by the GrIS into a varying number of elements (i.e., 100 < m < 4200) with varying levels 175

of covariance.  This exercise yielded highly unrealistic ice mass changes that nevertheless 176

provided a good fit to the SSH rates observed offshore Greenland. An example is shown in 177

*Figure 2. The inverted model (Figure 2A) is characterized by a large zone of ice melt in south 178*

central Greenland peaking at rates of -4 m/yr and ice growth focused entirely on the margins of 179

the ice sheet. This pattern is at odds with observations of GrIS mass change, which in general 180

show ice mass loss along the coast and ice mass gain in the interior (e.g., Shepherd et al., 2020, 181

Velicogna et al., 2020, Simonsen et al., 2021). The equivalent global mean sea level change of 182

this inverted ice model is 0.8 mm/yr across the interval 1993-2019. The predicted SSH rates 183

explain 84% of the variance in the observations (Figure 2B). For a more comprehensive 184

discussion of the non-uniqueness issue related to SSH inversions, see Bao et al. (2025). 185

4. Conclusions 323

Coulson et al. (2022) established a robust detection of the sea level fingerprint of Greenland Ice 324

Sheet mass flux by comparing modeling predictions of SSH rates generated using ice altimeter 325

estimates of the mass flux with ocean altimeter observations of these rates in the vicinity of the 326

island, up to 78°N. However, this detection leaves unanswered a key question; namely, what is 327

the information content, or, alternatively, the resolving power of the SSH rates in any inference 328

of ice mass changes? We have explored this issue via a suite of Bayesian inversions of the 329

observed SSH changes. A first conclusion is that inferences of ice mass changes based upon SSH 330

rates encircling Greenland are highly non-unique, and sensible results require the incorporation 331

of a-priori constraints on the ice mass flux. However, a second conclusion is that relatively 332

objective constraints are sufficient to produce an inference of ice mass flux that is consistent with 333

independent constraints on GrIS mass balance over the past three decades at the length scale of 334

the Greenland Ice Sheet, and tentatively, relative contributions at the drainage-basin scale in the 335

southern GrIS where SSH coverage is more extensive. 336

Analyses presented herein indicate that this second conclusion is relatively insensitive to the 337

mask applied to avoid near shore SSH observations (i.e., a 50 km or 100 km mask) which are 338

subject to a range of inaccuracies. In contrast, accurate inferences of ice mass flux require a 339

correction for the dynamic sea level signal in the SSH observations, such as the correction 340

performed in Coulson et al. (2022), and show some sensitivity to the long-term GIA correction 341

applied. Our analysis represents the first effort to directly invert SSH observations for ice mass 342

changes and suggests that the consideration of such data, particularly in combination with other 343

data sets (e.g., ocean reanalysis products that provide a robust estimate of ocean dynamics, tide 344

gauges, GRACE gravity, ice altimeter measurements, GNSS observations) has the potential to 345

improve constraints on ice sheet mass changes in a warming world. 346
